summary: Records experiences with operational requirements for ENUM-based softswitches, collected from a pre-commercial trial run by the National Internet Development Agency of Korea in 2006 between two Korean VoIP carriers. It notes considerations for call routing and suggests an interim approach that keeps existing commercial softswitches stable. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a report from a trial where two phone companies tried connecting calls using phone-number lookups. It shares what they learned so others avoid the same troubles.

subtitle: Operational lessons from an ENUM trial connecting Korean VoIP carriers.

tldr.problem: VoIP carriers need efficient ways to route calls between networks and handle number portability. ENUM (E.164 to URI mapping through DNS) offers a long-term solution but requires massive DNS population before it becomes practical.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5346 documents a 2006 trial where two Korean VoIP carriers tested ENUM-based call routing using a centralized ENUM DNS server, combining ENUM lookups with traditional prefix-based PSTN routing as a fallback.
tldr.outcome: The trial showed that ENUM can work reliably in hybrid mode without impacting call setup latency, providing a practical interim approach while DNS ENUM data is still sparsely populated.

today: RFC 5346 is Informational and documents experiences from the 2006 ENUM trial. It remains relevant to understanding the practical deployment challenges of Infrastructure ENUM and the hybrid approaches needed during the transition to DNS-based call routing.

sections.title: The ENUM Challenge
sections.content:
ENUM (E.164 to Uniform Resource Identifiers mapping) is a DNS-based system that converts phone numbers into internet contact information. Instead of a carrier needing pre-configured connections to every other carrier, ENUM allows softswitches to look up a phone number in DNS and discover how to reach it. However, this long-term approach requires massive DNS population across carriers.

The challenge is the transition period: when only a few carriers have provisioned numbers into ENUM, most lookups will fail, forcing softswitches to fall back on traditional prefix-based routing through the PSTN. This document reports experiences from a pre-commercial trial conducted by the National Internet Development Agency of Korea (NIDA) in 2006, which explored how to operate ENUM-enabled softswitches during this interim period without disrupting existing VoIP services.
sections.eli5: When everyone uses DNS to find phone numbers, you can connect calls easily. But at first, few numbers are in DNS. How do you start using ENUM when it's still mostly empty?

sections.title: Call Routing on Softswitches
sections.content:
A softswitch is a computer-based telephone switch that processes phone numbers, determines how to route calls, and initiates connections. When a call arrives, the softswitch must discover routing information: where is the destination number reachable? Traditional softswitches use a routing table based on number prefixes (the first digits of the phone number) to make this decision.

With ENUM, a softswitch can query DNS instead: given the E.164 telephone number, return the SIP or H.323 URI for reaching it. The challenge is that in the early stages of ENUM deployment, most numbers will not be in DNS. If a softswitch exclusively uses ENUM, it will fail for the majority of calls. Therefore, an interim solution must combine ENUM lookups (for the growing set of provisioned numbers) with traditional prefix-based routing (for everything else).
sections.eli5: Old way: look at the first digits of the number, decide where to send it. New way: ask DNS where this number is. In between: try DNS first, then fall back to old way if DNS doesn't know.

sections.title: Infrastructure ENUM Trial in Korea
sections.content:
NIDA, which manages Korea's +82 country code space (2.8.e164.arpa), organized a trial in 2006 with two VoIP service providers. The trial created a centralized ENUM DNS system operated by NIDA, and both carriers built ENUM modules into their softswitches. The carriers provisioned their trial users' phone numbers using Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP), and changes were pushed to the ENUM DNS immediately using DNS Dynamic Update (RFC 2136).

The trial system included separate EPP-based provisioning infrastructure. The carriers did not integrate it into their existing customer provisioning systems, which were mission-critical and owned by each carrier separately. This separation allowed the trial to proceed without risking existing commercial systems.
sections.eli5: Two Korean phone companies connected their systems to a shared DNS run by the government agency. They entered their numbers into it and let it update automatically. Everything was separate from their real production systems.

sections.title: Operational Rules for ENUM Lookups
sections.content:
The trial established specific policies for different types of phone number ranges. For "ENUM only" ranges (where numbers could only be reached via Internet, not the PSTN), if a number was in service, a valid SIP or H.323 URI had to be in ENUM. If the number was not in service, the ENUM domain would exist but contain no valid URIs, signaling to the softswitch that the call should fail immediately (not fall back to PSTN).

When the ENUM DNS responded with Rcode 0 (success), the softswitch could either use the returned URI or discover that no usable URI was present. When the DNS responded with Rcode 3 (name error) or other errors, the softswitch would fall back to traditional PSTN routing using the E.164 number. For numbers with PSTN Points of Interconnect, the domain routing could use either a fixed internal table (mapping domain names to specific carrier gateways) or DNS lookups, with the trial softswitches configured to switch between approaches if needed.
sections.eli5: Different number types have different rules: some can only go through the Internet (so fail immediately if not in DNS), some can go through old phone lines (so fall back if DNS doesn't know). The softswitch follows these rules automatically.

sections.title: Trial Results and Considerations
sections.content:
The trial measured call setup latency (answer delay time) comparing ENUM-based and non-ENUM routing. Results showed that calls using ENUM took roughly the same time as traditional routing, with differences under one second in all cases. This demonstrated that ENUM does not introduce unacceptable delays, enabling it to work reliably for commercial VoIP service.

However, the trial raised important considerations about centralized ENUM management: who is responsible for routing errors when shared DNS data is incorrect? When number portability is added, determining which carrier should fix incorrect ENUM data becomes unclear. Additionally, carriers questioned whether Infrastructure ENUM must be publicly accessible via the Internet or could operate privately between carriers. These considerations suggest that ENUM modules in softswitches need flexibility to adapt as policies and agreements evolve during the interim period.
sections.eli5: The trial worked: ENUM calls were just as fast as regular calls. But managing shared DNS is tricky when something goes wrong. And should everyone see the phone numbers, or should it be private between carriers?
